Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.

Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.

- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 21 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Progressively worsening right scrotal pain and swelling over 3 days, uncomfortable with walking, unrelieved by acetaminophen.
Analysis: The patient presents with acute-onset, progressively worsening right scrotal pain and swelling without fever, dysuria, hematuria, or discharge. Physical exam shows right hemiscrotal swelling with tenderness of the right testis and epididymis, intact bilateral cremasteric reflexes, and no inguinal tenderness. Testicular Doppler ultrasonography demonstrates normal echogenicity with significantly increased vascularity of the right testicle/epididymis compared to the left, plus a small reactive hydrocele. This pattern is classic for acute epididymitis (or epididymo-orchitis), with increased flow effectively excluding testicular torsion (which would show decreased or absent flow). The patient is sexually active with multiple partners and does not use condoms, making sexually transmitted epididymitis (Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae) the most likely etiology. Normal urinalysis and absence of systemic symptoms argue against a urinary tract source or systemic infection. The differential includes testicular torsion (excluded by Doppler), testicular tumor (unlikely given acute pain and inflammatory findings), and trauma (denied).
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Results of pending STD panel and urine culture; repeat scrotal examination if symptoms worsen.
Conclusion: Acute right-sided epididymitis, most likely sexually transmitted, confirmed by Doppler ultrasonography showing increased vascularity and reactive hydrocele, with torsion effectively ruled out.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Urology
Recommendations: Initiate empiric antibiotic therapy for sexually transmitted epididymitis (e.g., single-dose ceftriaxone plus a 10–14 day course of doxycycline) after obtaining the pending STD panel and urine culture results. Provide scrotal support, elevation, and analgesics (e.g., NSAIDs) for symptom relief. Advise sexual abstinence until treatment is complete and partners are evaluated/treated; recommend condom use. Arrange follow-up to review STD panel and urine culture results and confirm clinical improvement. Reassure the patient that torsion has been excluded by imaging; instruct him to return immediately if pain becomes severe or sudden, or if fever develops.
Notes: Increased vascularity on Doppler is the key finding distinguishing epididymitis from testicular torsion; the intact cremasteric reflexes and absence of fever support this diagnosis. Pending STD results should guide antibiotic adjustments if needed.

Vignette:
A 62-year-old woman with a history of osteoarthritis managed with daily naproxen for the past 3 years presents with a 4-week history of gnawing epigastric pain, early satiety, and occasional nausea. The pain is worse on an empty stomach and partially relieved by eating. She denies vomiting, hematemesis, melena, or unintentional weight loss. She does not smoke but drinks one glass of wine nightly. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination reveals mild epigastric tenderness on deep palpation without rebound or guarding. Bowel sounds are normoactive. There is no hepatosplenomegaly. A fecal occult blood test is negative. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 12.1 g/dL.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 62  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: 4-week history of gnawing epigastric pain, early satiety, and occasional nausea; pain worse on empty stomach and partially relieved by eating.  
Analysis: The patient has chronic NSAID use (naproxen for 3 years) and symptoms typical of peptic ulcer disease (PUD) or gastritis: gnawing epigastric pain, early satiety, nausea, pain on empty stomach relieved by eating. No red flags (no vomiting, hematemesis, melena, weight loss; negative fecal occult blood; hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL is borderline low but not frankly anemic). Differential includes NSAID-induced PUD, gastritis, functional dyspepsia, and less likely gastric malignancy given the absence of weight loss and negative FOBT. The clinical picture is consistent with uncomplicated NSAID-related dyspepsia/PUD.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Upper endoscopy (EGD), H. pylori testing (stool antigen or urea breath test), complete blood count (already obtained).  
Conclusion: Likely NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease or gastritis; requires further diagnostic evaluation and management, but no emergent intervention is indicated.  
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology  
Recommendations: Discontinue naproxen (consider alternative analgesia for osteoarthritis, e.g., acetaminophen or topical agents). Initiate a proton pump inhibitor (e.g., omeprazole 20 mg daily) for 4–8 weeks. Test for H. pylori and treat if positive. Arrange outpatient upper endoscopy to confirm diagnosis and exclude malignancy. Advise limiting alcohol intake. Schedule follow-up in 2–4 weeks to assess symptom response; if symptoms persist or worsen, reassess.  
Notes: None

baseline_protocol:
Age: 40  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Difficulty falling and staying asleep for the past 5 nights, with daytime fatigue and difficulty concentrating, in the context of work-related stress and anxiety.  
Analysis: The patient presents with acute insomnia (5 nights) temporally linked to a stressful work deadline and associated anxiety. He denies depressed mood, loss of interest, or suicidal ideation, and has no prior sleep disorder history. Caffeine consumption until mid-afternoon may contribute to sleep disruption. Physical examination, vital signs, neurological exam, and mental status exam are unremarkable. Differential considerations include adjustment disorder with anxiety, acute stress reaction, primary insomnia, and caffeine-related sleep disturbance. No red flags (e.g., mood disorder, substance use, medical comorbidity) are present. The condition is self-limiting and amenable to non-pharmacologic management.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None (no additional tests are indicated at this time; if symptoms persist beyond 2–3 weeks, consider a sleep diary, screening for mood disorders, and referral for polysomnography if sleep apnea or other sleep disorders are suspected).  
Conclusion: Acute insomnia related to stress and anxiety, with caffeine as a contributing factor. No evidence of major depressive disorder, suicidal ideation, or other urgent pathology.  
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Psychiatry  
Recommendations: 1) Implement sleep hygiene: maintain a consistent sleep-wake schedule, avoid screens 1 hour before bed, ensure a dark, quiet, and cool sleep environment. 2) Limit caffeine: avoid all caffeine after noon; consider eliminating it entirely during this period. 3) Stress management: practice relaxation techniques (e.g., deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation), mindfulness, and brief cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) strategies such as stimulus control and sleep restriction. 4) Address work stress: consider time management, delegation, or discussing the deadline with a supervisor if feasible. 5) If symptoms persist beyond 1–2 weeks, schedule a follow-up with a primary care provider or mental health professional; short-term use of a non-benzodiazepine hypnotic (e.g., zolpidem) may be considered only after clinician discussion, but is not first-line. 6) Seek immediate medical attention if new symptoms develop, including depressed mood, hopelessness, or suicidal ideation.  
Notes: None (essential caveat: if insomnia persists for more than 3 months, evaluate for chronic insomnia disorder and consider further workup for underlying causes such as sleep apnea or restless legs syndrome).

Vignette:
A 5-year-old girl is brought to the clinic by her parents for a spreading rash around her mouth and nose that began 5 days ago. It started as a small red spot near her left nostril and has since developed into multiple crusty lesions. Several children at her daycare have had similar sores. She is otherwise well with no fever, sore throat, or decreased appetite. On examination, there are multiple well-defined erosions with thick golden-yellow (honey-colored) crusts clustered around the nares and upper lip, with two satellite lesions on the left cheek. The lesions range from 1 to 3 cm in size. There is no warmth, fluctuance, or deep tissue involvement. There is mild left submandibular lymphadenopathy. The remainder of the skin examination is normal. She has no history of eczema or immunodeficiency.

Sex: Female  
Complaint: Spreading rash around mouth and nose with honey-colored crusts for 5 days.  
Analysis: The clinical presentation is classic for non-bullous impetigo: well-defined erosions with thick golden-yellow crusts clustered around the nares and upper lip, satellite lesions, daycare exposure, and absence of fever or systemic symptoms. The mild submandibular lymphadenopathy is consistent with localized infection. No signs of deeper tissue involvement (no warmth, fluctuance, or deep involvement) or eczema/immunodeficiency. Differential diagnoses include herpes simplex (typically vesicular, not honey-colored crusts), tinea faciei (scaly, annular), and contact dermatitis, but the honey-colored crusts and daycare exposure strongly favor impetigo.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None (clinical diagnosis; culture only if atypical or treatment failure).  
Conclusion: Non-bullous impetigo (likely Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes) in a well child.  
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology  
Recommendations: Initiate topical antibiotic therapy (e.g., mupirocin 2% ointment applied to lesions three times daily for 5–7 days). Advise good hand hygiene, avoid scratching, and keep lesions covered. Cleanse affected areas gently with soap and water. Reassure parents that lesions are contagious until crusts resolve; keep child home from daycare until crusts are dry or after 24 hours of treatment. Consider oral antibiotics (e.g., cephalexin) if lesions are extensive or if topical therapy fails.

Vignette:
An 8-year-old girl is brought to the pediatrician by her mother for intense itching that has been worsening over the past 2 weeks. The itching is particularly severe at night and disrupts her sleep. Her mother reports that her younger brother and father have recently developed similar itching. On examination, there are numerous small erythematous papules and excoriations in the interdigital web spaces of both hands, the flexor surfaces of the wrists, the axillary folds, and the periumbilical area. Several short, linear burrows approximately 5 to 10 mm in length are visible in the web spaces between the fingers. The face and scalp are spared. There are no vesicles or bullae. baseline_protocol:
Age: 8-year-old girl
Sex: Female
Complaint: Intense itching worsening over 2 weeks, worse at night, disrupting sleep; similar itching in younger brother and father.
Analysis: The clinical presentation is classic for scabies. Key supporting facts include: severe nocturnal pruritus, involvement of interdigital web spaces, flexor wrists, axillary folds, and periumbilical area with sparing of face and scalp; presence of short linear burrows; and confirmation by mineral oil preparation showing mites, eggs, and fecal pellets. The family history of similar itching supports contagious transmission. Differential considerations include other pruritic dermatoses (e.g., atopic dermatitis, contact dermatitis, insect bites, papular urticaria), but the burrows and microscopic findings are pathognomonic for scabies. No vesicles or bullae rule out bullous disorders. The condition is not emergent and can be managed on an outpatient basis.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None (diagnosis already confirmed by microscopy; no further tests needed).
Conclusion: Scabies infestation (Sarcoptes scabiei) in an 8-year-old girl with household transmission.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Treat the patient and all household contacts (including asymptomatic family members) simultaneously with permethrin 5% cream applied from neck down (face/scalp spared in this case) and left on for 8–14 hours, then washed off. Repeat application after 7 days. Wash all clothing, bedding, and towels used in the past 3 days in hot water and dry on high heat; items that cannot be washed should be sealed in plastic bags for at least 72 hours. Provide symptomatic relief with oral antihistamines (e.g., cetirizine) for itching, especially at night. Advise that pruritus may persist for up to 2–4 weeks after successful treatment due to residual hypersensitivity. Educate the family on hygiene measures and the need to treat all close contacts to prevent reinfestation. Schedule a follow-up visit in 2–4 weeks to confirm resolution or assess for treatment failure.

Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.

Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.

Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.

Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.

- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,

chest. It is not worsened by exertion, movement, food, activity, or respiration. She also had
shortness of breath and chills but no cough, nausea, or diaphoresis. She took 400 mg of
naproxen without relief. The pain has persisted, prompting her to come to the emergency

take her temperature.

Skin: Noncontributory

HEENT: No recent URI symptoms.

has noted dyspnea with climbing stairs since chest pain began; dyspnea resolves quickly with
rest and is not worsened by lying flat.

normal.

Genitourinary: Minimal spotting after recent menses.

Musculoskeletal: She has no current musculoskeletal symptoms, although she has noted
intermittent left leg swelling and discomfort for the past year. There is no history of injury or

recent immobilization. The last time she had swelling and discomfort in her left leg was about 10
days ago.

Neurologic: Noncontributory

Psychiatric: Noncontributory

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Menorrhagia due to uterine fibroids, with secondary iron-deficiency anemia;
endometriosis; right breast fibroadenoma. No history of blood clots or clotting disorder.

Surgical history: Laparoscopy and lysis of adhesions for endometriosis; tubal ligation; excision
of breast fibroadenoma.

Medications: None

Allergies: None

Family history: Mother was recently diagnosed with stage IV colon carcinoma; brother has
schizophrenia.

General appearance: Appears anxious and in some pain. No cyanosis or respiratory distress.

Pulse 107 beats/min

Respirations: 16/min
O2 saturation 96% on room air

Musculoskeletal: No joint deformity, full range of motion without pain. Lower extremities: no

Neurologic: Cranial nerves intact; muscle strength and sensation intact throughout.

Mental status: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time.

Results of appropriate laboratory testing return and show:
Serum D-dimer level: 395 ng/mL [2.16 nmol/L]
Hemoglobin: 9.7 g/dL
Platelets: 330,000/mcL

Sex: Female  
Complaint: Sudden onset of sharp left-sided chest pain radiating to the center of the chest, with shortness of breath and chills.  
Analysis: The patient presents with acute chest pain, dyspnea, and tachycardia. CT pulmonary angiography shows filling defects in bilateral segmental pulmonary arteries, confirming acute pulmonary embolism. Supporting findings include elevated D-dimer (395 ng/mL), tachycardia (107 bpm), and a history of intermittent left leg swelling (possible DVT). Differential considerations include acute coronary syndrome (troponin normal, ECG not shown but no ischemic changes described), aortic dissection (no blood pressure differential or pulse deficit), and musculoskeletal pain (pain not worsened by movement or respiration). The CT finding is definitive for PE.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None (CT pulmonary angiography already performed; further testing not required for immediate management).  
Conclusion: Acute bilateral segmental pulmonary embolism.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology  
Recommendations: Initiate therapeutic anticoagulation (e.g., unfractionated heparin or low-molecular-weight heparin) without delay. Admit to an inpatient unit for monitoring and ongoing care. Assess hemodynamic stability and consider echocardiography to evaluate for right ventricular strain if clinically indicated. Manage pain with appropriate analgesics (avoid NSAIDs given potential bleeding risk with anticoagulation). Address the patient's anemia (hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL) and menorrhagia, as anticoagulation may increase bleeding risk; monitor for bleeding and consider gynecologic consultation. Evaluate for underlying hypercoagulable state after acute treatment, given the history of leg swelling and no prior clotting disorder.

Vignette:
A 72-year-old man with a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia and recent urinary tract infection treated with oral antibiotics presents with 2 days of worsening confusion, fever, and decreased oral intake. His wife reports he has been increasingly lethargic and today was unable to recognize her. On examination, he is obtunded, with warm, flushed skin. Vital signs: T 39.4C, HR 122, RR 26, BP 76/44 (MAP 55), SpO2 93% on room air. Suprapubic tenderness is present with a distended bladder. Foley catheter insertion yields 800 mL of cloudy, foul-smelling urine. Labs: WBC 24,800/mcL with 22% bands, creatinine 3.2 mg/dL (baseline 1.2), lactate 5.8 mmol/L, procalcitonin 48 ng/mL, platelets 82,000/mcL. Urinalysis shows too numerous to count WBC and bacteria. SOFA score is 11. Blood and urine cultures are obtained, and broad-spectrum antibiotics and IV fluid resuscitation are initiated.

Age: 72
Sex: Male
Complaint: Two days of worsening confusion, fever, and decreased oral intake; now obtunded with hypotension, tachycardia, and signs of septic shock.
Analysis: The patient presents with septic shock secondary to urosepsis. Strong supporting facts include high fever (39.4°C), tachycardia (HR 122), tachypnea (RR 26), hypotension (BP 76/44, MAP 55), obtundation, warm flushed skin, suprapubic tenderness with a distended bladder yielding 800 mL of cloudy foul-smelling urine, marked leukocytosis with bandemia (WBC 24,800, 22% bands), elevated lactate (5.8 mmol/L), markedly elevated procalcitonin (48 ng/mL), acute kidney injury (creatinine 3.2 vs baseline 1.2), thrombocytopenia (platelets 82,000), and a SOFA score of 11. The urinary tract is the most likely source given the recent UTI, BPH with bladder outlet obstruction, and pyuria/bacteriuria. Differential considerations include other sepsis sources (pneumonia, intra-abdominal infection), but the clinical and laboratory findings strongly support urosepsis with septic shock and end-organ dysfunction (AKI, altered mental status, coagulopathy).
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Renal/bladder ultrasound or CT abdomen-pelvis to assess for urinary obstruction, abscess, or calculi; repeat lactate and blood gas; coagulation panel; chest X-ray to exclude alternate source; central venous access for vasopressor administration; continuous hemodynamic and urine output monitoring.
Conclusion: Septic shock from urosepsis with acute kidney injury, thrombocytopenia, and altered mental status. The patient requires immediate aggressive resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and source control (bladder decompression and evaluation for obstruction). High risk of mortality without urgent intervention.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency
Recommendations: Continue broad-spectrum antibiotics (already initiated) and aggressive IV fluid resuscitation; initiate vasopressors (norepinephrine first-line) to target MAP ≥65 mm Hg if hypotension persists despite fluids. Maintain Foley catheter drainage and monitor urine output. Obtain urgent imaging (renal ultrasound or CT) to evaluate for urinary obstruction or abscess and arrange urology consultation for source control. Admit to ICU. Repeat lactate, creatinine, and platelet counts; monitor for worsening AKI, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and respiratory failure. Reassess volume status and consider early de-escalation of antibiotics once cultures and sensitivities return.
Notes: This is a life-threatening emergency with a high SOFA score (11) and septic shock; do not delay ICU transfer or source control. The underlying BPH-related bladder outlet obstruction must be addressed to prevent recurrent urosepsis. None

Age: 68 years  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: One-week worsening dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, lower extremity edema, cough with white sputum, wheezing, and 3-kg weight gain in a patient with known mild heart failure.  
Analysis: The patient presents with subacute worsening of heart failure symptoms (dyspnea, orthopnea, edema, weight gain) in the setting of a recent diagnosis of mild heart failure. Physical examination reveals elevated jugular venous pressure, bibasilar crackles, an S3 gallop, a holosystolic murmur consistent with mitral regurgitation, and pitting edema to the thighs. Laboratory testing shows markedly elevated BNP (1420 pg/mL) with a normal troponin. Echocardiography demonstrates preserved LVEF (55%) with severe concentric LV hypertrophy, restrictive diastolic filling (E/A>2, reduced e’ velocities), biatrial enlargement, and mild mitral regurgitation. The fat pad biopsy shows Congo red–positive, apple-green birefringent amorphous deposits, confirming amyloidosis. The combination of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, restrictive physiology, macroglossia, and biopsy-proven amyloid deposition strongly suggests cardiac amyloidosis. The patient also has a history of MGUS, raising concern for AL (light-chain) amyloidosis. Differential considerations include other causes of restrictive cardiomyopathy (e.g., sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis, constrictive pericarditis), but the biopsy is diagnostic. The absence of fever, chest pain, and hemodynamic instability, along with stable oxygen saturation, indicates that this is not an acute emergency but requires prompt, coordinated evaluation and management in a monitored setting.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 50  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Persistent heartburn and acid regurgitation for 6 months despite omeprazole 20 mg daily, worse after meals and when lying down, with nocturnal symptoms (sour taste, coughing) and dental enamel erosion.  
Analysis: The patient has classic symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) that are refractory to standard-dose PPI therapy. Supporting facts include obesity (BMI 34), symptom exacerbation by large meals and recumbency, nocturnal regurgitation with cough, and dental enamel erosion (a sign of chronic acid exposure). The absence of alarm features (dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, hematemesis) reduces the likelihood of complicated disease but does not exclude it. Differential considerations include refractory GERD (inadequate acid suppression, rapid PPI metabolism, or non-acid reflux), eosinophilic esophagitis, gastroparesis, or functional heartburn. Given the persistent symptoms despite appropriate PPI use, further diagnostic evaluation is warranted.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Upper endoscopy (EGD) with biopsy; if EGD is normal, ambulatory esophageal pH-impedance monitoring (off PPI) and esophageal manometry; consider Helicobacter pylori testing if not previously done.  
Conclusion: This is a case of PPI-refractory GERD in an obese patient with typical symptoms and extraesophageal manifestations (cough, enamel erosion). No emergency findings are present, but the condition requires further diagnostic workup and management adjustment in a healthcare setting.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology  
Recommendations: 1) Optimize PPI therapy: increase to double dose (e.g., omeprazole 40 mg twice daily) taken 30–60 minutes before meals, or switch to a more potent PPI (e.g., esomeprazole). 2) Reinforce lifestyle measures: weight loss, avoid large meals, elevate head of bed, avoid alcohol and late meals. 3) Perform upper endoscopy to assess for erosive esophagitis, Barrett’s esophagus, or other pathology. 4) If endoscopy is negative, consider pH-impedance monitoring to document acid/non-acid reflux and correlate symptoms. 5) Address dental enamel erosion: refer to dentist for protective measures (e.g., fluoride application). 6) Reassess after 4–8 weeks; if symptoms persist, consider esophageal manometry to rule out motility disorders.  
Notes: The absence of alarm symptoms is reassuring, but refractory GERD warrants endoscopic evaluation to exclude complications. Obesity is a major contributing factor; weight reduction should be emphasized. Alcohol consumption may worsen reflux and should be minimized.

Vignette:
A 28-year-old woman presents with pain on the index finger of her left hand after accidentally touching a hot pan while cooking approximately 1 hour ago. She ran the finger under cool water immediately. She denies blistering, numbness, or limited range of motion. On examination, there is diffuse erythema of the palmar surface of the left index finger from the fingertip to the proximal interphalangeal joint. The skin is intact with no blistering or blanching. The area is tender to light touch and warm. Capillary refill is less than 2 seconds. Sensation and range of motion of the finger are intact.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 28
Sex: Female
Complaint: Pain on the palmar surface of the left index finger after accidental contact with a hot pan approximately 1 hour prior.
Analysis: The patient sustained a thermal injury to the left index finger. Examination shows diffuse erythema from the fingertip to the proximal interphalangeal joint with intact skin, no blistering or blanching, tenderness to light touch, and warmth. Capillary refill is less than 2 seconds, and sensation and range of motion are intact. These findings are consistent with a first-degree (superficial) burn. The absence of blistering, blanching, numbness, or restricted motion rules out partial-thickness or full-thickness burns. Immediate cooling was already performed. No signs of infection or neurovascular compromise are present. Differential considerations include superficial partial-thickness burn (excluded by lack of blistering) and deeper thermal injury (excluded by intact sensation, normal capillary refill, and absence of blanching).
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: First-degree superficial thermal burn of the palmar left index finger, self-limiting, with intact skin integrity and normal neurovascular function. No complications identified.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Continue to cool the area with cool (not ice-cold) water or a clean cool compress for pain relief. Apply a bland emollient or moisturizer (e.g., aloe vera or petrolatum) to soothe the skin. Over-the-counter oral analgesics (e.g., acetaminophen or ibuprofen) may be used for pain as needed. Avoid further heat exposure, tight bandages, or popping any blisters should they develop. Keep the area clean and monitor for signs of infection (increasing redness, swelling, purulent drainage, or fever). Reassure the patient that symptoms typically resolve within a few days; seek medical evaluation if pain worsens, blistering develops, or signs of infection appear.
Notes: None

Age: 26  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: 3-day history of sharp, steady lower abdominal pain radiating bilaterally, with new nausea and vomiting, fever, and urinary symptoms (frequency, incomplete emptying) in an 18-week pregnant woman.  
Analysis: The patient is an 18-week pregnant woman with fever (38.8°C), tachycardia (120 bpm), bilateral costovertebral angle tenderness, and urinalysis showing pyuria, bacteriuria, nitrites, and leukocyte esterase, consistent with acute pyelonephritis. She also has signs of dehydration (dry mucous membranes, ketonuria, inability to keep down fluids). Pregnancy increases the risk of complications from pyelonephritis, including sepsis, preterm labor, and renal dysfunction. Differential considerations include lower urinary tract infection, appendicitis, ovarian torsion, and other abdominal pathology, but the combination of fever, CVA tenderness, and positive urinalysis strongly supports pyelonephritis. The absence of cervical motion tenderness and normal fetal heart rate are reassuring but do not exclude the diagnosis. Given the systemic symptoms and pregnancy, urgent hospitalization for IV antibiotics and hydration is required.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Urine culture and sensitivity, blood cultures, complete blood count with differential, serum electrolytes and renal function tests, and fetal monitoring (non-stress test or biophysical profile).  
Conclusion: Acute pyelonephritis in pregnancy with systemic symptoms and dehydration. Requires emergent care and inpatient management.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Obstetrics and Gynecology  
Recommendations: Admit to hospital for IV antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone or ampicillin plus gentamicin, adjusted for pregnancy), IV fluid resuscitation, antipyretics, and antiemetics. Obtain urine and blood cultures before initiating antibiotics. Monitor maternal vital signs, urine output, and fetal heart rate. Provide supportive care for nausea and vomiting. Consider infectious disease consultation if no clinical improvement within 48 hours. Educate on signs of preterm labor.  
Notes: Pregnancy increases the risk of complications; prompt treatment is essential. Avoid nephrotoxic drugs and adjust antibiotic dosing for renal function. Monitor for sepsis and preterm labor.

A 50-year-old man presents with intermittent burning sensation in the substernal area that he has experienced occasionally over the past several weeks. The burning typically occurs 30 to 60 minutes after large meals, particularly those that are spicy or high in fat. The discomfort is relieved within minutes by over-the-counter antacids. He denies dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, hematemesis, or melena. He has no cardiac history. On examination, vital signs are normal. The abdomen is soft, non-tender, and non-distended. Age: 50
Sex: Male
Complaint: Intermittent burning substernal sensation occurring 30-60 minutes after large, spicy, or fatty meals, relieved by over-the-counter antacids.
Analysis: The clinical presentation is highly consistent with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). The postprandial timing, association with large/spicy/fatty meals, and prompt relief with antacids are classic features. The absence of dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, hematemesis, or melena rules out alarm symptoms that would warrant urgent endoscopic evaluation. Physical examination is unremarkable, with no epigastric tenderness or cardiac abnormalities. Differential considerations include peptic ulcer disease (less likely given the substernal location and antacid response) and cardiac ischemia (unlikely given no cardiac history, normal vital signs, and relief with antacids, though atypical presentations should be kept in mind). No red flags are present, and the condition appears benign and self-limited.

Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology

Age: 12 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Intermittent mild upper back pain and stiffness for about one year, without functional limitation or red-flag symptoms.
Analysis: The patient is a prepubertal (Tanner stage 3) boy with mild thoracic paraspinous tenderness and a positive forward-bend test showing shoulder asymmetry and scapular prominence. Spine X-ray confirms a right thoracic and left lumbar scoliosis with a Cobb angle of 11°, no bony lesions, and no sacroiliitis. The absence of fever, night pain, neurologic deficits, leg-length discrepancy, joint hypermobility, and abnormal body proportions (upper/lower ratio 1.06, wingspan/height 0.98) strongly supports adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. The mild, non-limiting pain is consistent with this diagnosis and lacks red flags for infection, tumor, or inflammatory disease. Differential considerations include congenital scoliosis (excluded by X-ray), neuromuscular scoliosis (excluded by normal neurologic exam), and Scheuermann kyphosis (not suggested by imaging or exam). Given the low Cobb angle and absence of concerning features, this is a benign, self-limited condition requiring observation rather than urgent intervention.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None (initial X-ray already performed; follow-up imaging and clinical monitoring can be scheduled as recommended by a specialist).
Conclusion: Mild adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (Cobb angle 11°) with no evidence of underlying pathology or functional impairment. The condition is stable and non-urgent.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics
Recommendations: Reassure the patient and family that the scoliosis is mild and unlikely to cause significant problems. Refer to a pediatric orthopedic or spine specialist for formal evaluation and to establish a monitoring plan. Given the patient's remaining growth potential (Tanner stage 3), schedule clinical re-examination and repeat spine X-ray in 6–12 months to assess for curve progression. Encourage normal physical activity and sports without restriction. For mild pain, recommend over-the-counter analgesics (e.g., acetaminophen or ibuprofen) as needed, and advise the patient to return if pain worsens, becomes nocturnal, or is accompanied by neurologic symptoms, fever, or weight loss. No bracing or surgical intervention is indicated at this time.

Vignette:
A 19-year-old female college student is brought in by her roommate with a 24-hour history of high fever, diffuse rash, vomiting, profuse watery diarrhea, and progressive lightheadedness. She reports using a menstrual tampon that she forgot to change for approximately 3 days. On examination, she appears acutely ill with a diffuse, blanching, erythematous macular rash resembling a sunburn covering the trunk and extremities, including the palms and soles. Vital signs: T 40.2C, HR 136, RR 26, BP 72/40, SpO2 94%. Mucous membranes are hyperemic. Pelvic exam reveals a retained tampon, which is removed, and there is no evidence of abscess. Labs: WBC 15,400/mcL, platelets 88,000/mcL, creatinine 2.8 mg/dL, AST 245 U/L, ALT 198 U/L, CK 1,240 U/L. Blood cultures are drawn and empiric clindamycin and vancomycin are initiated.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 19
Sex: Female
Complaint: 24-hour history of high fever, diffuse sunburn-like rash, vomiting, profuse watery diarrhea, and progressive lightheadedness in the setting of a retained menstrual tampon for approximately 3 days.
Analysis: The presentation is highly consistent with menstrual toxic shock syndrome (TSS) caused by Staphylococcus aureus producing the TSST-1 superantigen. Strong supporting facts include prolonged tampon retention, high fever (40.2°C), diffuse blanching erythematous rash involving palms and soles, hyperemic mucous membranes, and hypotension (BP 72/40) with tachycardia (HR 136) indicating septic shock. Multi-organ dysfunction is evident: acute kidney injury (creatinine 2.8 mg/dL), transaminitis (AST 245, ALT 198), thrombocytopenia (platelets 88,000), and elevated CK (1,240) suggesting muscle injury. Differential considerations include streptococcal toxic shock syndrome, staphylococcal bacteremia, meningococcemia, and other causes of sepsis; however, the tampon association, rash pattern, and shock strongly favor menstrual TSS. Blood cultures were drawn and empiric clindamycin (to suppress toxin synthesis) and vancomycin were appropriately initiated.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Serum lactate, arterial blood gas, coagulation panel (PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer), continuous hemodynamic monitoring, urine output measurement, vaginal/cervical cultures for S. aureus, and repeat renal and hepatic function panels.
Conclusion: Menstrual toxic shock syndrome complicated by septic shock and multi-organ dysfunction (renal, hepatic, hematologic, muscular). This is a life-threatening emergency requiring aggressive resuscitation and intensive care.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Infectious Disease
Recommendations: Admit to the intensive care unit. Initiate aggressive IV fluid resuscitation with crystalloids to restore perfusion; add vasopressors (e.g., norepinephrine) if hypotension persists despite fluids. Continue empiric clindamycin (to inhibit toxin production) and vancomycin; consider adding a beta-lactam antistaphylococcal agent (e.g., oxacillin/nafcillin) if methicillin-susceptible S. aureus is suspected or confirmed. Ensure complete removal of the retained tampon (already performed) and obtain cultures from blood, vagina, and cervix. Monitor closely for complications including ARDS, DIC, and progressive renal failure; consider IVIG in cases of refractory shock. Provide supportive care for vomiting and diarrhea with electrolyte replacement and maintain strict input/output monitoring.
Notes: TSS is a clinical diagnosis; blood cultures may be negative in a substantial proportion of cases because TSST-1 acts as a superantigen. Early source control (tampon removal) and prompt antibiotic therapy are critical determinants of outcome.

Vignette:
A 32-year-old male singer presents with a hoarse voice that has persisted for 3 days following an intense concert performance. He reports mild sore throat and throat dryness but denies dyspnea, stridor, dysphagia, fever, or hemoptysis. He is a non-smoker and does not consume alcohol regularly. He has no history of GERD or thyroid disease. On examination, he is afebrile. The oropharynx is mildly erythematous without exudates or lesions. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy. His voice is notably hoarse and breathy. Respiratory effort is normal with no stridor or wheezing on auscultation.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 32
Sex: Male
Complaint: Hoarse, breathy voice persisting for 3 days after an intense concert performance, accompanied by mild sore throat and throat dryness.
Analysis: The patient is a young, otherwise healthy singer who developed acute hoarseness immediately following intense vocal exertion (concert performance). The breathy quality of the voice suggests vocal fold edema, mucosal irritation, or possible phonotrauma from vocal overuse. Supporting facts include the clear temporal relationship to vocal strain, absence of fever, absence of exudates or lesions on oropharyngeal exam, and no cervical lymphadenopathy. The absence of dyspnea, stridor, dysphagia, fever, and hemoptysis effectively rules out serious airway compromise, epiglottitis, and significant infectious pathology. His non-smoking status and lack of GERD or thyroid disease reduce the likelihood of chronic organic causes. The main differential considerations include acute laryngitis (viral or irritative), vocal fold edema/hemorrhage from phonotrauma, and functional dysphonia; chronic conditions such as vocal fold nodules, Reinke's edema, or vocal fold paresis are less likely given the acute onset but should be considered if symptoms persist.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Flexible laryngoscopy (recommended if hoarseness persists beyond 1–2 weeks or if vocal fold hemorrhage is suspected); otherwise, no immediate diagnostic testing is required.
Conclusion: Acute laryngitis/phonotrauma secondary to vocal overuse in a singer. The presentation is benign and self-limited, with no clinical indicators of airway compromise or serious infection.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)
Recommendations: Advise strict voice rest (avoid speaking, singing, and whispering, as whispering can further strain the vocal folds). Encourage adequate oral hydration, use of a humidifier or steam inhalation to soothe the throat, and avoidance of throat clearing (substitute with sips of water). Avoid caffeine and alcohol, which can dehydrate the mucosa. No antibiotics or systemic steroids are indicated given the absence of infection signs. If hoarseness persists beyond 2 weeks, worsens, or if the patient develops dyspnea, stridor, dysphagia, or hemoptysis, refer promptly to an ENT specialist for laryngoscopic evaluation.
Notes: Vocal fold hemorrhage should be considered in a singer with sudden severe hoarseness after intense performance; if suspected, urgent ENT evaluation and complete voice rest are warranted. Otherwise, the condition is expected to resolve with conservative management.

Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.

It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.

Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Vignette:
A 53-yr-old woman comes to the office because of palpitations. She is a current patient there
and has a history of well-controlled hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and tension headaches. She
states that she has noticed intermittent palpitations over the past 2 mo. She describes the
episodes as a sensation of irregular and racing heartbeats that are accompanied by fatigue.
She denies any chest pain, shortness of breath, light-headedness, or syncope. The episodes
last from 10 min to several hours, occur once or twice/wk, and resolve on their own. The last
episode was 3 days ago. She cannot identify any particular triggers. She is generally active and
walks 3 miles several days/wk without any exertional symptoms including chest pain and
dyspnea. She has no family history of early cardiac disease or sudden death. She denies any
recent fever or infectious symptoms.

Review of Systems:
General: Patient has generally been feeling fine.

Skin: No new rashes or skin lesions.

HEENT: No vision changes, ear pain, nasal symptoms, or sore throat.

Pulmonary: Denies shortness of breath, dyspnea during exertion, and cough.

Cardiovascular: No orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or lower-extremity edema.

Gastrointestinal: Denies abdominal pain and poor appetite.

Genitourinary: Noncontributory

Reproductive: Noncontributory

Musculoskeletal: No recent injury.

Neurologic: Noncontributory

Psychiatric: Has been generally in good spirits; no extremes of mood.

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and tension headaches.

Surgical history: Appendectomy at age 20.

Medications: Lisinopril 10 mg daily and metformin 500 mg bid.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Family history: Mother is alive and has hypertension and diabetes mellitus. Father died of lung
cancer. No history of early coronary artery disease or sudden cardiac death.

Social history: Patient is married and works as a school teacher. Regularly exercises 3
times/wk. No history of smoking. Drinks a glass of wine with dinner most nights and one cup of
coffee each morning. Denies use of decongestants, cocaine, and other stimulants. No illicit drug
use.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Slender middle-aged woman in no apparent distress.

Vital signs:
Temperature: 37.2° C
Pulse: 58 beats/min
BP: 125/74 mm Hg
Respirations: 14/min
Oxygen saturation: 96% on room air

Skin: No rashes noted.

HEENT: Oropharynx clear.

Pulmonary: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally. No wheeze, rhonchi, or rales.

Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Brisk carotid upstrokes. No jugular venous distention.

Gastrointestinal: Soft, nontender, nondistended abdomen; positive bowel sounds.

Genitourinary: Unremarkable

Musculoskeletal: Unremarkable

Neurologic: Unremarkable

Mental status: Unremarkable

Age: 53 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Intermittent palpitations (sensation of irregular and racing heartbeats) with fatigue over the past 2 months.
Analysis: The patient presents with intermittent palpitations lasting 10 minutes to several hours, occurring 1–2 times per week, and resolving spontaneously. She has no chest pain, dyspnea, lightheadedness, or syncope, and is asymptomatic during exertion. Her physical examination is normal, including a regular heart rate and rhythm, normal heart sounds, and no signs of heart failure. She has well-controlled hypertension and type 2 diabetes, which are risk factors for cardiovascular disease, but no family history of early cardiac disease or sudden death. The most likely differential diagnoses include benign arrhythmias (e.g., premature atrial or ventricular contractions, supraventricular tachycardia) or atrial fibrillation/flutter. Given the intermittent nature, ambulatory monitoring is needed to capture the arrhythmia. Other considerations include thyroid dysfunction, electrolyte imbalances, or stimulant use (denied). The absence of concerning symptoms and normal exam make an emergent condition unlikely.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: 12-lead ECG, ambulatory cardiac monitoring (Holter monitor or event monitor), thyroid function tests (TSH), serum electrolytes, and possibly echocardiography if arrhythmia is confirmed or structural heart disease is suspected.
Conclusion: The patient has symptomatic palpitations with a normal physical examination and no high-risk features. The likely cause is a paroxysmal arrhythmia, most commonly atrial fibrillation or supraventricular tachycardia, which requires outpatient diagnostic evaluation to confirm and guide management. No immediate emergency intervention is indicated.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Cardiology
Recommendations: Arrange outpatient cardiology consultation. Obtain a 12-lead ECG at the next visit and consider a 24–48 hour Holter monitor or longer event monitor to document the rhythm during symptoms. Check thyroid function and serum electrolytes. Advise the patient to keep a symptom diary and note any triggers (e.g., caffeine, alcohol, stress). Continue current antihypertensive and antidiabetic medications; ensure blood pressure and glucose are well controlled. If the arrhythmia is confirmed, further management (e.g., rate control, anticoagulation if atrial fibrillation) should be guided by cardiology. Reassure the patient that no urgent intervention is needed, but she should seek immediate care if she develops chest pain, syncope, or severe dyspnea.

A 72-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history and known COPD (GOLD stage II) presents with a 5-day history of increased sputum production and mild worsening of his baseline dyspnea. He reports his sputum has changed from white to yellow-green. He denies fever, chest pain, hemoptysis, or significant increase in cough frequency. He is currently using tiotropium and an albuterol rescue inhaler as needed. Vital signs show temperature 98.6°F, heart rate 82, blood pressure 134/78, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 93% on room air (baseline 94-95%). Sex: Male  
Complaint: Increased sputum production with purulent change (yellow-green) and mild worsening of baseline dyspnea in a patient with known COPD.  
Analysis: The patient has GOLD stage II COPD and presents with a classic acute exacerbation: increased sputum volume, purulence, and worsening dyspnea. He is afebrile, has no chest pain, hemoptysis, or significant cough increase. Vital signs are stable; oxygen saturation is 93% on room air, only slightly below his baseline of 94–95%. Examination shows mild bilateral expiratory wheezing without accessory muscle use, and he speaks in full sentences, indicating no severe respiratory distress. The purulent sputum suggests a bacterial component, warranting antibiotic therapy. Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology

Educate the patient on warning signs (increasing dyspnea, fever, confusion) and to seek emergency care if these occur. Consider chest X-ray to rule out pneumonia.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 72 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Generalized dry, itchy skin worsening over several weeks during winter, most severe on shins and forearms; daily hot water bathing with regular bar soap.
Analysis: The presentation is consistent with xerosis (winter itch) exacerbated by environmental dryness and irritant bathing practices. Key supporting facts: onset in winter, distribution on extremities, diffuse dryness with fine scaling and superficial cracking, absence of rash, excoriations, erythematous plaques, papules, jaundice, or lymphadenopathy. No systemic symptoms (weight loss, jaundice) or new medications suggest a benign, localized skin condition. Differential considerations include atopic dermatitis, contact dermatitis, scabies, and systemic causes of pruritus (e.g., cholestasis, renal failure, thyroid disease), but these are less likely given the absence of characteristic findings and the clear environmental/behavioral triggers.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None (clinical diagnosis; no additional tests indicated based on history and examination).
Conclusion: Xerosis (dry skin) with pruritus, likely due to cold, dry winter air and irritant bathing habits (hot water, bar soap). No evidence of secondary infection, inflammatory dermatosis, or systemic disease.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: 
- Advise patient to reduce bathing frequency to once daily or less, using lukewarm (not hot) water and limiting bath time to 5–10 minutes.
- Replace regular bar soap with a mild, fragrance-free, moisturizing cleanser; apply only to axillae, groin, and feet if needed.
- Pat skin dry gently and apply a thick, fragrance-free emollient (e.g., petrolatum-based ointment or cream) immediately after bathing and at least twice daily, especially on shins and forearms.
- Use a humidifier in the home to increase ambient humidity.
- Wear soft, breathable fabrics (cotton) and avoid wool or rough materials directly on skin.
- If itching persists despite these measures, consider a short course of low-potency topical corticosteroid or oral antihistamine, but only after reassessment.
- Reassure that this is not a serious condition; schedule follow-up in 2–4 weeks if symptoms do not improve or if new lesions, excoriations, or systemic symptoms develop.

Age: 20  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Bilateral dull, aching pain along the front of both shins occurring during and shortly after running, resolving with rest.  
Analysis: The patient presents with bilateral medial tibial pain that is activity-related and resolves with rest, with no pain at rest, nighttime pain, swelling, or point tenderness. No red flags for emergent or urgent conditions are present.

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics

Vignette:
A 17-year-old female is brought in by her parents after they discovered an empty bottle of extra-strength acetaminophen (500 mg tablets, 50-count) in her room. She admits to intentionally ingesting approximately 25 grams 12 hours ago following a breakup. She initially felt fine but now reports nausea, vomiting, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. On examination, she is tearful but cooperative. Vital signs: T 37.2C, HR 96, RR 18, BP 112/68, SpO2 99%. Abdomen is tender in the right upper quadrant. Scleral icterus is not yet present. Labs: acetaminophen level 180 mcg/mL (well above treatment line on Rumack-Matthew nomogram at 12 hours), AST 1,240 U/L, ALT 1,086 U/L, INR 1.8, total bilirubin 2.1 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, pH 7.34, lactate 2.8 mmol/L. N-acetylcysteine infusion is initiated immediately. Psychiatry and social work consultations are placed. Poison control is contacted.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 17
Sex: Female
Complaint: Intentional acetaminophen overdose (approximately 25 g ingested 12 hours prior) presenting with nausea, vomiting, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain.
Analysis: The patient ingested a massive, potentially lethal dose of acetaminophen (25 g, far exceeding the hepatotoxic threshold). The 12-hour serum acetaminophen level of 180 mcg/mL is well above the Rumack-Matthew nomogram treatment line, confirming toxicity. Laboratory findings demonstrate established acute hepatocellular injury (AST 1,240 U/L, ALT 1,086 U/L), early coagulopathy (INR 1.8), and elevated total bilirubin (2.1 mg/dL), indicating significant hepatotoxicity. Mild metabolic acidosis (pH 7.34) with elevated lactate (2.8 mmol/L) raises concern for early hepatic dysfunction and possible progression to fulminant hepatic failure. Differential considerations include fulminant hepatic failure from acetaminophen, other causes of acute liver injury (e.g., viral or ischemic hepatitis), and co-ingestants. NAC infusion has been appropriately initiated, and psychiatry, social work, and poison control have been engaged.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Serial liver function tests (AST, ALT, total bilirubin), INR/coagulation panel, serum pH and lactate, renal function/creatinine, serum glucose, continuous vital sign and neurologic monitoring; repeat acetaminophen levels; comprehensive urine toxicology screen for co-ingestants.
Conclusion: Severe acute acetaminophen toxicity with established hepatotoxicity and early coagulopathy, at risk for progression to fulminant hepatic failure; requires ongoing emergent management with NAC and close monitoring.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency
Recommendations: Continue IV N-acetylcysteine infusion per established protocol without interruption. Monitor liver enzymes, INR, bilirubin, pH, lactate, glucose, and renal function serially (every 6–12 hours initially). Assess frequently for signs of fulminant hepatic failure, including hepatic encephalopathy, worsening coagulopathy, hypoglycemia, and progressive acidosis. Maintain euglycemia and provide supportive care (IV fluids, antiemetics). Consider early transfer to a liver transplant center if clinical deterioration occurs. Complete psychiatry and social work evaluation for suicide risk and safety planning. Maintain contact with poison control for ongoing guidance.
Notes: The INR of 1.8 and markedly elevated transaminases indicate significant liver injury; absence of scleral icterus does not exclude severe toxicity. Peak hepatic injury may not yet have occurred, so serial monitoring is critical.

Age: 70
Sex: Male
Complaint: 18 hours of worsening right upper quadrant pain, fever with rigors, and progressive jaundice.

The presence of septic shock with end-organ hypoperfusion mandates immediate intervention.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology
Recommendations: Initiate aggressive IV fluid resuscitation and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam or ceftriaxone plus metronidazole) immediately after blood cultures. Arrange urgent ERCP for biliary drainage within hours, as antibiotics alone are insufficient; consider percutaneous or surgical drainage if ERCP is unavailable or fails. Add vasopressors if hypotension persists despite fluids. Admit to ICU for monitoring of hemodynamics, urine output, and serial lactate. Address the prior sphincterotomy history, which increases risk of recurrent stone disease and may complicate cannulation. Monitor for complications including cholangitic abscess, perforation, acute kidney injury, and coagulopathy.

- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Vignette:
A 3-year-old girl is brought in by her mother with a low-grade fever of 37.8°C and small blisters noticed on her hands and feet since this morning. The mother also notes a few small sores inside the child's mouth. The child is eating and drinking well, though slightly fussier than usual. Several children at her daycare have had similar symptoms. On examination, there are scattered small vesicles on the palms, soles, and a few on the dorsal hands. Two shallow ulcers are seen on the buccal mucosa. The child is alert, playful, and well-hydrated.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 3 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Low-grade fever (37.8°C), small blisters on hands and feet, and a few sores inside the mouth.
Analysis: The clinical presentation of low-grade fever, vesicular lesions on the palms, soles, and dorsal hands, along with shallow oral ulcers in a young child with known daycare exposure to similar symptoms, is highly consistent with hand-foot-mouth disease (HFMD), typically caused by coxsackievirus (e.g., enterovirus). The child is alert, playful, and well-hydrated, with good oral intake, indicating a mild, uncomplicated course. Differential considerations include other viral exanthems (e.g., herpes simplex stomatitis, varicella) or allergic reactions, but the characteristic distribution and epidemiology strongly favor HFMD. No red flags (e.g., dehydration, lethargy, high fever, neurological signs) are present.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None (clinical diagnosis is sufficient; no laboratory or imaging studies are indicated in this typical, mild presentation).
Conclusion: Mild hand-foot-mouth disease (HFMD) in a well-hydrated, clinically stable child. Self-limiting viral illness with no need for emergency intervention.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics
Recommendations: Provide supportive care at home: ensure adequate fluid intake (offer cool fluids, avoid acidic or salty foods), use acetaminophen or ibuprofen (dosed by weight) for fever or discomfort if needed. Maintain good hand hygiene to prevent spread. Monitor for signs of dehydration (decreased urination, dry mouth, lethargy) or complications (high fever, stiff neck, difficulty waking, seizures) and seek medical attention if these develop. The child may return to daycare once fever resolves and lesions are dry (typically 5–7 days). No antiviral therapy or antibiotics are indicated.

The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.
